case.title: Separate necessary from sufficient conditions — analyze

messages.content: A simplified model states that every person with condition C tests positive, but some people without C can also test positive. Analyze the argument that a positive result proves C in this model.
The test never misses C in this simplified model.
Which part of your account are you least certain about?
So any positive result logically proves C; the stated false positives do not affect that inference.

response.rationale: The learner explicitly reverses the stated implication and dismisses the positive-without-C premise. plan.targetQuote: So any positive result logically proves C; the stated false positives do not affect that inference.
plan.rubricItem: Distinguishes the condition implying a positive result from a positive result establishing the condition.
plan.objective: Assess whether the learner can analyze how the stated model bears on the claimed inference from a positive result to C, without confusing it with the no-misses implication.
plan.scenario: The existing simplified screening model states that every person with C tests positive and that some people without C can also test positive. The learner says any positive result logically proves C and dismisses the stated false positives.
assumptions: Use only the two statements in the simplified model, not real-world screening performance or prevalence.
A result proving C means that the result establishes C in every case allowed by the model.
heldFixed: Every person with C tests positive.
The model allows positive results for some people without C.
The task is theoretical analysis of the learner's universal inference.
varied: The learner's reasoning about whether the model supports their positive-result-to-C inference.
plan.construction: Ask: "You said that any positive result logically proves C. How does the model's statement about people without C affect that claim? Explain how your reasoning fits with the fact that everyone with C tests positive." Do not supply a particular counterexample or state whether the claim is valid.
plan.prerequisitesSatisfied: The transcript supplies both logical relationships and an explicit claimed conclusion. The learner has already correctly identified the no-false-negatives relationship, so the targeted analysis requires no new domain law or numerical method.
limitations: A correct verdict without an explanation does not establish that the learner distinguishes the two directions.
An unclear response could reflect terminology confusion or failure to integrate a premise rather than a general difficulty with implication.
This local probe does not establish transfer to other conditional arguments.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner distinguishes the two implication directions and integrates the stated positive-without-C cases.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Explains that an allowed positive result without C defeats the universal claim, while everyone with C can still test positive.
responseSignals.interpretation: Evidence of the targeted distinction and model-based analysis in this setting.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner continues to treat the no-misses relationship as reversible.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Defends positive results as proof of C because everyone with C tests positive, without explaining how positive-without-C cases can coexist with that conclusion.
responseSignals.interpretation: Tentative evidence of continued reversal or failure to integrate the premise; the precise mechanism remains uncertain.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner reaches a verdict but does not demonstrate the targeted reasoning.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Retracts the claim or says false positives matter without connecting the allowed cases to the universal claim and the no-misses statement.
responseSignals.interpretation: The answer alone leaves the distinction between implication directions unresolved.
